messages.content: What are the different properties of Hydrogen?

message.content:
**Hydrogen – Key Properties** | Property | Value / Description | |----------|---------------------| | **Chemical Symbol** | H | | **Atomic Number** | 1 | | **Atomic Mass** | ~1.008 u (average; varies by isotope) | | **Isotopes** | Protium (^1H), Deuterium (^2H), Tritium (^3H) | | **Electron Configuration** | 1s¹ | | **Electronegativity (Pauling)** | 2.20 | | **First Ionization Energy** | 13.598 eV | | **Electron Affinity** | –0.754 eV (negative, so it does not readily accept an extra electron) | | **Molecular Form** | Diatomic molecule H₂ under normal conditions | | **Boiling Point** | –252.9 °C (−423.8 °F) | | **Melting Point** | –259.2 °C (–434.2 °F) | | **Density (at STP)** | 0.08988 g/L (≈0.00008988 g/cm³) | | **State at Room Temperature** | Gas | | **Color / Odor / Taste** | Colorless, odorless, tasteless | | **Magnetic Moment** | Paramagnetic (due to one unpaired electron in H₂⁺) | | **Electrical Conductivity** | Poor conductor in neutral form; becomes conductive when ionized (plasma) | | **Flammability** | Extremely flammable; reacts violently with oxygen to form water (combustion) | | **Reducing Agent** | Strong reducing agent (especially in its atomic or ionic forms) | | **Bond Dissociation Energy (H–H)** | 436 kJ/mol (104 kcal/mol) | | **Specific Heat Capacity (gas, 25 °C)** | 14.304 J/(mol·K) | | **Heat of Formation (H₂(g))** | 0 kJ/mol (by definition) | | **Standard Enthalpy of Combustion** | –285.83 kJ/mol (for H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O(l)) | | **Standard Gibbs Free Energy of Formation** | –237.13 kJ/mol (for H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O(l)) | | **Uses** | • Rocket propellant (liquid hydrogen)
• Fuel cell technology (electrochemical conversion to electricity)
• Chemical feedstock (ammonia synthesis, methanol production, hydrogenation reactions)
• Metallurgical processes (reducing agent, hydrogen embrittlement studies)
• Cryogenics (storage of liquefied gases)
• Medical imaging (contrast agents, MRI)
• Fundamental research (stellar nucleosynthesis, plasma physics) | --- ### Quick Takeaways * Hydrogen is the lightest element, existing naturally as a diatomic gas (H₂) at standard conditions. * Its most common isotope, protium, has no neutrons; deuterium and tritium add one and two neutrons respectively. * It’s highly reactive, forming stable compounds with many elements (e.g., water, ammonia, hydrocarbons). * In industrial settings, hydrogen is produced mainly by steam‑methane reforming, electrolysis of water, or partial oxidation of natural gas. * Because of its low density and high reactivity, handling requires careful safety measures (ventilation, explosion-proof equipment). Feel free to ask if you’d like deeper details on any specific property or application!
